paper.title_en: Quantum active matter: An operational framework for mechanisms and evidence
paper.abstract_en: Work on quantum active matter often runs together two different claims: that an active process has been realized in a quantum system, and that changing a specific quantum resource, such as a coherence, a correlation, or exchange statistics, changes the active behaviour. The first claim does not imply the second, because a quantum system can still behave as a classical active system would. A recent single-atom experiment illustrates this. Spin-exchange collisions deliver motional energy in discrete quanta, yet the resulting motion is reproduced by a parameter-free classical active Langevin model: the first claim holds, while the second has not yet been tested. This critical, selective Review supplies an operational vocabulary that keeps the two claims apart, intended to be useable by soft-matter and quantum-physics readers alike. The activity axis, A0–A2, asks whether active-like behaviour is observed, whether its mechanism is closed at a stated system boundary, and whether its statistics are generated endogenously. The quantum-function axis, Q0–Q2, asks whether a quantum formalism or implementation is specified, whether a specific quantum resource is present during operation, and whether a matched intervention shows that the resource changes an active observable. A separate, optional certification records whether a prespecified class of classical models is excluded; it is not a higher universal level of “quantumness”. We compare representative single-particle and many-body routes, distinguish effective operators, conditioned trajectories, and trace-preserving dynamics, and give practical tests based on matched interventions, classical null models, thermodynamic uncertainty relations, temporal inequalities, and predictive process models. Robust quantum implementations and several endogenous quantum-enabled active processes are now established. What remains open is the causal question: showing, quantitatively and reproducibly, when coherence, exchange statistics, correlations, or measurement backaction changes autonomous transport or collective organization.
